title: Sleep: the setting that runs the others
note: Four parts per chapter, as in the Direction: the moment, inside you, the reset, back to default. Gaps after chapter ends are the planned quiet between chapters.

lines.chapter: Opening
say: It's 3:07 a.m. and you're awake again.

lines.chapter: Opening
say: You checked the time twice.
Both times, it was later than you hoped.

lines.chapter: Opening
say: In four hours, an alarm goes off.
You'll get up, and you'll blame the night.

lines.chapter: Opening
say: Sleep is the setting that runs the others.
Tonight, three questions about it.

lines.chapter: Opening
say: Why am I always tired?
How do I fall asleep faster?
And why is it always three a.m.?

lines.chapter: 1. Why am I always tired?
say: Seven a.m. The alarm.
You slept. You're still tired.

lines.chapter: 1. Why am I always tired?
say: Before you blame your age, your job or your genes, check the three things you control.

lines.chapter: 1. Why am I always tired?
say: One: short sleep.
Adults need seven hours or more a night.
About one in three get less.

lines.chapter: 1. Why am I always tired?
say: All day, a chemical called adenosine builds up in your brain.
It comes from the energy your brain burns, and it's one of the signals that make you sleepy.

lines.chapter: 1. Why am I always tired?
say: Sleep clears it.
Cut sleep short, and you start the day with yesterday's leftovers.

lines.chapter: 1. Why am I always tired?
say: Two: late coffee.
Caffeine doesn't clear adenosine.
It sits in the spots adenosine needs and switches nothing on.
The sleepiness is still there. You just can't feel it.

lines.chapter: 1. Why am I always tired?
say: Your body clears half the caffeine in about five hours, on average.
In some people it's an hour and a half. In others, nine and a half.

lines.chapter: 1. Why am I always tired?
say: A coffee at six p.m.? About half of it is still in you at eleven.
You're not a light sleeper. You're caffeinated.

lines.chapter: 1. Why am I always tired?
say: A review of twenty-four studies found caffeine cost about forty-five minutes of sleep.
For a regular cup, it put the cut-off at almost nine hours before bed.

lines.chapter: 1. Why am I always tired?
say: In one small study, four cups' worth, six hours before bed, cut sleep by more than an hour.

lines.chapter: 1. Why am I always tired?
say: Three: late light.
Your brain has a clock, and it runs mostly on light and dark.
In the evening it releases melatonin, the signal that it's night.

lines.chapter: 1. Why am I always tired?
say: Ordinary room light, in the eight hours before bed, delayed melatonin in ninety-nine percent of people, and shortened it by about ninety minutes.

lines.chapter: 1. Why am I always tired?
say: Reading on a glowing tablet instead of a paper book pushed the body clock later, and added about ten minutes to falling asleep.

lines.chapter: 1. Why am I always tired?
say: So your sleep signal comes later.
Your alarm doesn't.

lines.chapter: 1. Why am I always tired?
say: For a seven a.m. alarm: in bed by eleven.
Last coffee by two.
Lights low from eight.

lines.chapter: 1. Why am I always tired?
say: Eight hours in bed, for seven of sleep.
Even good sleepers take a while to drop off, and wake a little in the night.

lines.chapter: 1. Why am I always tired?
say: Still tired after all that? See a doctor.
Low iron, your thyroid or sleep apnoea can cause it, and coffee fixes none of them.

lines.chapter: 2. How do I fall asleep faster?
say: Eleven p.m. Lights off. Eyes open.
You work out how much sleep you'll get if you fall asleep now.
And now.

lines.chapter: 2. How do I fall asleep faster?
say: How long should it take? About ten to twenty minutes.
Thirty or less still counts as good sleep.
Out within a minute isn't a talent. It can mean you're short on sleep.

lines.chapter: 2. How do I fall asleep faster?
say: Caffeine again: in studies, it added about nine minutes to falling asleep.

lines.chapter: 2. How do I fall asleep faster?
say: Heat helps, which sounds backwards.
A warm bath or shower, one to two hours before bed, even for ten minutes, shortened the time to fall asleep in a review of seventeen studies.

lines.chapter: 2. How do I fall asleep faster?
say: The warmth draws blood to your hands and feet.
You shed heat, your core cools, and that drop is what helps.

lines.chapter: 2. How do I fall asleep faster?
say: Evening exercise didn't harm sleep across twenty-three studies.
The possible exception: a hard session that ends within an hour of bed.

lines.chapter: 2. How do I fall asleep faster?
say: Trying hard can backfire.
Students told to fall asleep fast, with marches playing, took thirty-four minutes. Those who didn't try: twenty-two.
With calm music, trying worked.

lines.chapter: 2. How do I fall asleep faster?
say: In one small study, five minutes writing a to-do list for the next few days got people to sleep faster than writing about what they'd already done.

lines.chapter: 2. How do I fall asleep faster?
say: In another, people with insomnia who pictured an engaging scene fell asleep faster than people given no instructions.

lines.chapter: 2. How do I fall asleep faster?
say: The viral tricks? The military method, the four-seven-eight breath: we found no trial that timed them.
The internet timed them for you.

lines.chapter: 2. How do I fall asleep faster?
say: Melatonin pills: about seven minutes faster, across nineteen studies.
American sleep doctors suggest not using them for insomnia.

lines.chapter: 2. How do I fall asleep faster?
say: Not asleep after twenty minutes? Get up.
Do something quiet, away from screens.
Go back when you're sleepy.

lines.chapter: 2. How do I fall asleep faster?
say: It feels like giving up.
It's part of CBT for insomnia, the first-line treatment.
Across twenty trials, people with insomnia fell asleep about nineteen minutes faster.

lines.chapter: 2. How do I fall asleep faster?
say: The usual list of sleep tips, on its own, isn't recommended as a treatment.
Inside CBT, it's one of the parts.

lines.chapter: 2. How do I fall asleep faster?
say: Over thirty minutes, at least three nights a week, for three months?
That may be insomnia. See a doctor.

lines.chapter: 3. Why do I wake up at 3 a.m.?
say: Three-oh-seven. Again.
Your body is asleep. Your mind has called a meeting.

lines.chapter: 3. Why do I wake up at 3 a.m.?
say: One waking in the night, back to sleep within twenty minutes, still counts as good sleep.

lines.chapter: 3. Why do I wake up at 3 a.m.?
say: Older adults wake three or four times a night on average, and notice it more.

lines.chapter: 3. Why do I wake up at 3 a.m.?
say: Sleep isn't one long dive.
It runs in cycles of about ninety minutes, four to six times a night.

lines.chapter: 3. Why do I wake up at 3 a.m.?
say: Deep sleep comes early, in the first half of the night.
REM sleep gets longer toward morning.

lines.chapter: 3. Why do I wake up at 3 a.m.?
say: So by three, most of your deep sleep is behind you.
And the sleep pressure that knocked you out at eleven has been draining for hours.

lines.chapter: 3. Why do I wake up at 3 a.m.?
say: Your body is already getting ready for the day.
Cortisol starts rising in the final hours of sleep.
It sets its alarm long before you do.

lines.chapter: 3. Why do I wake up at 3 a.m.?
say: Alcohol gets you to sleep faster and holds the first half of the night together.
Then it breaks up the second half, at every dose studied.
It doesn't knock you out. It knocks you out until three.

lines.chapter: 3. Why do I wake up at 3 a.m.?
say: At night your body makes less urine, so most people can sleep six to eight hours without a trip.
That's why sleep doctors say: drink less before bed.

lines.chapter: 3. Why do I wake up at 3 a.m.?
say: Stress, noise and a room that's too hot or too cold are on the NHS list of usual causes.

lines.chapter: 3. Why do I wake up at 3 a.m.?
say: Don't check the clock.
In two experiments, people told to watch a clock while trying to sleep worried more and took longer to fall asleep.
Turn it to the wall. It'll still be three-oh-seven.

lines.chapter: 3. Why do I wake up at 3 a.m.?
say: Can't get back to sleep? Same rule as bedtime.
Get up, keep the light low, do something quiet, go back when you're sleepy.

lines.chapter: 3. Why do I wake up at 3 a.m.?
say: And keep alcohol, tea and coffee out of the last six hours before bed.
That's the NHS rule, not ours.

lines.chapter: 3. Why do I wake up at 3 a.m.?
say: Waking like this three nights a week, for three months? That's chronic insomnia.
About one in ten people have it, and CBT is the first treatment.

lines.chapter: 3. Why do I wake up at 3 a.m.?
say: Loud snoring, gasping, or breathing that stops and starts can be sleep apnoea. See a GP.

lines.chapter: 3. Why do I wake up at 3 a.m.?
say: And if you wake very early and feel low most of the day, every day, for more than two weeks, see a GP.

lines.chapter: Your settings
say: Your three settings. Set them from your alarm.

lines.chapter: Your settings
say: Bedtime: eight hours before it.

lines.chapter: Your settings
say: Last coffee: nine hours before bed.

lines.chapter: Your settings
say: Lights: low for three hours before bed.

lines.chapter: Your settings
say: For a seven a.m. alarm: in bed by eleven, last coffee by two, lights low from eight.

lines.chapter: Your settings
say: And at three a.m.: no clock, no phone, no negotiating.
Get up, stay dim, go back when you're sleepy.

lines.chapter: End
say: Back to factory settings.

drake2013: Drake C et al. Caffeine effects on sleep taken 0, 3, or 6 hours before going to bed. J Clin Sleep Med 2013: 400 mg 6 h before bed cut total sleep by more than 1 hour

chang2015: Chang AM et al. Evening use of light-emitting eReaders negatively affects sleep, circadian timing, and next-morning alertness. PNAS 2015
brown2022: Brown TM et al. Recommendations for daytime, evening, and nighttime indoor light exposure. PLoS Biol 2022: low evening light for at least 3 hours before bed
nsf: National Sleep Foundation, What Is Sleep Quality? (falling asleep in 30 minutes or less; waking 1 time or less; awake 20 minutes or less after falling asleep)
medlineplus: MedlinePlus. Fatigue: causes, and when to contact a provider
ccdrerup: Cleveland Clinic newsroom, 22 Jun 2026, sleep psychologist Michelle Drerup, PsyD: about 10 to 20 minutes to fall asleep; within a minute may suggest sleep deprivation
haghayegh2019: Haghayegh S et al. Before-bedtime passive body heating by warm shower or bath to improve sleep: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Sleep Med Rev 2019;46:124-135: 17 studies; 40 to 42.5 C, 1 to 2 h before bed, as little as 10 min
stutz2019: Stutz J, Eiholzer R, Spengler CM. Effects of evening exercise on sleep in healthy participants: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Sports Med 2019;49:269-287: 23 studies; sleep might be impaired after vigorous exercise ending 1 h or less before bedtime
ansfield1996: Ansfield ME, Wegner DM, Bowser R. Ironic effects of sleep urgency. Behav Res Ther 1996;34(7):523-531: high mental load, trying 34.40 vs 21.80 min; low load, trying 15.55 vs 29.28 min
scullin2018: Scullin MK et al. The effects of bedtime writing on difficulty falling asleep: a polysomnographic study comparing to-do lists and completed activity lists. J Exp Psychol Gen 2018;147(1):139-146 (57 healthy young adults)
vierra2022: Vierra J et al. Effects of sleep deprivation and 4-7-8 breathing control on heart rate variability, blood pressure, blood glucose, and endothelial function. Physiol Rep 2022 (measured heart and blood measures, not time to fall asleep)
ferracioli2013: Ferracioli-Oda E, Qawasmi A, Bloch MH. Meta-analysis: melatonin for the treatment of primary sleep disorders. PLoS One 2013: 19 studies, 1683 subjects; sleep latency -7.06 min
aasm2017: Sateia MJ et al. Clinical practice guideline for the pharmacologic treatment of chronic insomnia in adults: an AASM guideline. J Clin Sleep Med 2017: suggests clinicians not use melatonin for insomnia (WEAK)
aasmhabits: American Academy of Sleep Medicine, Healthy Sleep Habits (Aug 2020): get out of bed after 20 minutes; reduce fluid intake before bedtime
trauer2015: Trauer JM et al. Cognitive behavioral therapy for chronic insomnia: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Ann Intern Med 2015;163(3):191-204: 20 studies, 1,162 participants; sleep onset latency improved by 19.03 min
aasm2021: Edinger JD et al. Behavioral and psychological treatments for chronic insomnia disorder in adults: an AASM clinical practice guideline. J Clin Sleep Med 2021: CBT-I (STRONG); stimulus control (CONDITIONAL); sleep hygiene not as a single therapy (CONDITIONAL)
aasminsomnia: AASM Sleep Education, Insomnia: chronic insomnia occurs at least three times per week and lasts for at least three months; about 10 percent of people have chronic insomnia
nhsinsomnia: NHS, Insomnia (reviewed 19 Mar 2024): common causes; do not drink alcohol, tea or coffee at least 6 hours before bed; when to see a GP
medlineplus-aging: MedlinePlus, Aging changes in sleep (7/15/2024): older people wake up an average of 3 or 4 times each night and are more aware of being awake
ninds: NINDS, Brain Basics: Understanding Sleep (reviewed 25 Feb 2025): cycles through the night; deep sleep in the first half; longer REM later; sleep drive
statpearls-sleep: Patel AK et al. Physiology, Sleep Stages. StatPearls 2024: about 4 to 6 cycles a night averaging 90 minutes
dijk1995: Dijk DJ, Czeisler CA. Contribution of the circadian pacemaker and the sleep homeostat to sleep propensity, sleep structure, electroencephalographic slow waves, and sleep spindle activity in humans. J Neurosci 1995 (slow-wave activity decreased in the course of all sleep episodes)
statpearls-cortisol: Kaur J et al. Physiology, Cortisol. StatPearls 2025: levels begin to rise during the final hours of sleep
ebrahim2013: Ebrahim IO et al. Alcohol and sleep I: effects on normal sleep. Alcohol Clin Exp Res 2013;37:539-549: at all dosages, faster sleep onset, a more consolidated first half and more disruption in the second half
medlineplus-nocturia: MedlinePlus, Urinating more at night (7/1/2025): less urine at night lets most people sleep 6 to 8 hours without urinating
tang2007: Tang NKY, Schmidt DA, Harvey AG. Sleeping with the enemy: clock monitoring in the maintenance of insomnia. J Behav Ther Exp Psychiatry 2007;38:40-55 (two experiments)
nhsapnoea: NHS, Sleep apnoea (reviewed 11 May 2026): symptoms and when to see a GP
nhsdepression: NHS, Depression in adults: symptoms (waking up very early; see a GP if symptoms most of the day, every day, for more than 2 weeks)
harvey2002: Harvey AG, Payne S. The management of unwanted pre-sleep thoughts in insomnia: distraction with imagery versus general distraction. Behav Res Ther 2002;40(3):267-277 (41 people with insomnia)
